description: Tier B — real bottle photographs. Reported every run, never gates CI. Small n, nondeterministic, live model. The gap between this number and Tier A's is the honest answer to 'does this work', and it is a published metric rather than an embarrassment. Six photographs are in golden/tier_b/photos; three are declared here. The other three (fireball, found_north, ipa_torn) are pinned as unit regressions in tests/test_real_photo_regressions.py and are not yet declared as scored rows.
capture_guide: 6-8 photographs total, shot with a phone, originals unedited.
Mixed commodity: at least one spirits, one wine, one malt.
Front AND back of at least two products — the government warning usually lives on the back, which is TC-16.
2-3 straight-on and well lit. These are the baseline; if these fail, nothing else matters.
One with flash on curved glass, so there is real specular glare (TC-12). Code cannot fake this, which is the whole reason Tier B exists.
Keep the HEIC originals. They exercise the HEIC path and give the ingest step real EXIF orientation to strip.

Ground truth is bootstrapped, not transcribed: run the label through the app, then confirm or correct each field by eye and record the corrected value here. Set ground_truth to hand_verified once a human has signed off on the row.

Known limitation, stated rather than papered over: warning-statement VIOLATIONS cannot appear here. A commercially approved label does not carry them by definition, so those cases stay simulated in Tier A.

labels.name: courtyard_rose_back
labels.notes: The first WINE in the corpus; every other photograph is spirits or malt, so the commodity rules had never been exercised against a real label. Warning is present, complete and legible to the eye, with a bold 'GOVERNMENT WARNING:' heading and regular body. Producer prints as 'PRODUCED AND BOTTLED BY THE COURTYARD WINERIES / NORTH EAST, PA 16428' across two lines with no comma after the name — which is the case that exposed the containment allowance only matching the joined 'Name, Address' form. Measured at 337x443, well under the 1568px high-resolution tier, which is itself worth keeping: it is what a downloaded product photo looks like. alcohol_content EXPECTS MISSING, and this row was wrong in the first version of this file. It expected Not applicable on the assumption that a wine without an ABV is exempt. 27 CFR 4.36(b) is narrower than that: a wine at or below 14% may print 'table wine' or 'light wine' IN LIEU of the alcohol statement. This label is designated 'Dry Rose' and carries neither, so the statement is required and its absence is a real finding. The pipeline was right and the expectation was wrong.

labels.name: bacardi151_glare_cropped_back
labels.notes: TC-12 and TC-14 in one frame: real specular glare blowing out the red WARNING band, and the government warning running off the right edge of the picture. This is the case the product must not get wrong, and today it does. Measured: class_type, alcohol_content and net_contents all come back MISSING. They are not missing — they are outside the frame. Missing is a finding against the LABEL and grounds to return an application; Unreadable is a statement about the PHOTOGRAPH. Reporting the second as the first is a false accusation, and it is the exact asymmetry the whole design is built around. The expectations here record what should happen, so the gap is reported every run rather than discovered later.

labels.name: growler_warning_rotated
labels.notes: An amber growler whose only printed label is the warning sticker, applied turned ninety degrees so the text runs vertically. Two things it exercises that nothing else does. The warning reads MATCH at 0.95 despite the rotation, which is worth pinning before someone 'optimises' the preprocessing. And the four fields that genuinely are not on this container come back Missing, which is correct and is the counterpart to the Bacardi row: Missing when the element is absent, Unreadable when the picture is at fault. net_contents is embossed into the glass rather than printed, so Unreadable is the honest answer for it.
